title: Your PRD Isn't Done Until It Passes These 5 Questions
description:
A PRD isn't finished when you've written every section. It's finished when it survives the same review a design and engineering team would put it through. This Short walks the self-review checklist from the Level 1 capstone project: one build interpretation instead of many, testable acceptance criteria, non-goals specific enough to stop a scope-creep fight, a numeric success metric with a baseline, and a problem statement that stands on its own. Run your draft through it before you call it done.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/product-manager-mastery-path/level-1/10-project-complete-prd/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Here's why PRDs get stuck in review. It's not done when it's written. It's done when it passes these five questions.
One. Would two different engineers read this and build roughly the same thing? If there's room for very different interpretations, you're not done.
Two and three. Does every user story have acceptance criteria you can test against? Are your non-goals specific enough to stop a scope-creep argument, not just generic filler?

display.heading: 2-3 - Testable and specific
display.subheading: Acceptance criteria you can test - non-goals that block scope creep

beats.narration: Four and five. Is your success metric an actual number with a stated baseline? And could someone who doesn't know the backstory read your problem statement and get why it matters?

display.heading: 4-5 - Numeric metric, clear problem
display.subheading: A number with a baseline - a problem statement that stands alone

beats.narration: That's the same bar a real design and engineering review holds it to. Fix anything that doesn't hold up.

display.heading: The design-review bar
display.subheading: Revise anything that doesn't hold up
